opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, construction zones are one of my favorite examples of the long tail, because they look simple at first and then you realize they're full of subtlety.

Part of it is perception. Cones, barrels, temporary signs, lane shifts painted over old markings, the old lines still faintly visible. You have to figure out which cues are authoritative right now and which are leftovers. A map helps a lot in normal driving, but in a construction zone the world has changed relative to the map, so the system has to detect that and lean on what it actually sees.

Then there's the semantic layer, which is harder. A cone isn't just an obstacle. A line of cones tells you where the drivable corridor is. It might close a lane, or merge you into an oncoming lane that's temporarily been repurposed. You have to infer the intent of whoever set up the zone, often from fairly sparse and sometimes inconsistent evidence.

The human traffic director is a different flavor. Now you're interpreting gestures: a flagger with a stop/slow paddle, a police officer waving you through a red light, someone just pointing. Those gestures override the normal rules of the road, and they vary a lot from person to person. So you need models that understand human pose and intent, and that also reason about who has authority. A construction worker waving their arm to a colleague is not a signal for you.

The way we tend to think about it is that you can't hand-engineer your way through all of this. You need a lot of data, which means mining your fleet logs for these rare situations, and you need learned models that capture structure and context rather than just detecting objects. Simulation matters a lot too, because you want to test many variations of a scenario: different cone layouts, different gestures, other drivers behaving badly around the zone, and you can't wait to see all of those on the road.

And you need the system to know when it's uncertain. Sometimes the right behavior is to slow down, be conservative, maybe ask for remote assistance with a high-level hint, rather than confidently committing to a wrong interpretation. Handling these cases gracefully, not just correctly in the common case, is a big part of what makes driving safe at scale.

r001.rationale: The response says a line of cones may close a lane or merge traffic into an oncoming lane temporarily repurposed, identifying cones as a reason to cross ordinary lane boundaries.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and it gets at something that I think is really central to how we think about the problem at Waymo. Construction zones are one of those cases where the world deviates from the map, and deviates from the normal rules of the road, and so the car can't just rely on prior knowledge. It really has to perceive and understand what's going on in the scene in real time.

So there are a few layers to it. The first is perception. You need to detect the cones, the barriers, the signage, the construction vehicles, the workers, and you need to do it robustly. Cones are actually a nice example because they're small, they come in a lot of shapes and colors, they get knocked over, they get stacked, and they show up in lighting and weather conditions you've never quite seen before. So that's where having a lot of diverse data, and increasingly, large models that generalize well, really matters.

But detection alone isn't enough. The second layer is semantics. A line of cones isn't just a set of objects, it's a message. It's telling you the lane is closed, or the lane has shifted, or you need to merge. So you have to infer the intended path through the zone, which often means reasoning about a drivable corridor that doesn't correspond to any lane markings on the map. We've invested a lot in representing that kind of implied geometry, and in having the planner be comfortable operating in a space where the map is essentially a prior that can be overridden.

And then the human traffic director is the hardest piece, because now you're in the realm of understanding people. A person holding a slow sign or a stop sign, or waving you through, is communicating intent with gestures that can be pretty ambiguous. Is that wave meant for me or for the truck next to me? Did they just adjust their hat, or did they tell me to go? Humans resolve this with a lot of context and sometimes with eye contact. For the car, it means combining pose estimation, gesture understanding, and scene context, and critically, being conservative when the signal is uncertain. The right behavior is often to slow down, wait, and let the situation clarify, rather than committing on a low-confidence interpretation.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that this is where the long tail really shows up. You can drive millions of miles and still encounter a construction configuration you haven't seen before. So we lean heavily on simulation, where we can take real-world encounters and perturb them, move the cones around, change the worker's behavior, and test how the system responds across many variations. And we're increasingly seeing that models trained on broad, large-scale data, including a lot of structured knowledge about how the world works, generalize better to these novel situations than hand-engineered rules ever could.

So I'd say the way I think about it is less as a special-case problem and more as a stress test for general scene understanding. If your system can handle a chaotic construction zone with a human directing traffic, it's probably handling a lot of other things well too.

r001.rationale: The response says cones can indicate a closed or shifted lane and that the car may follow a path outside mapped lane markings, but it never clearly says the cones may lead the car to cross lane boundaries it would ordinarily respect.

astra-6.text:
Construction is an interesting example because you can’t simply assume that the road looks the way it did when you mapped it. The cones may be taking you out of your normal lane, and a person may be directing you to do something that’s different from what the traffic light is telling you. You need to interpret what’s happening right now.

There are several pieces to that. You have to perceive the cones and barriers, understand how they define a path, and recognize that there’s a person who is actually directing traffic. Then you have to interpret their gestures in context. Are they asking you to stop? Are they waving you through? Is that signal intended for you or for the car coming the other way?

The challenge is bringing that understanding into the driving decision, including the uncertainty. If the situation is ambiguous, you need to be able to slow down or stop rather than commit to a maneuver you don’t understand. And construction sites vary tremendously, so the goal is to build a system that can reason about those elements together and generalize to arrangements it hasn’t encountered before.

r001.rationale: It says cones may take the car out of its normal lane, clearly conveying that construction cones can require crossing ordinary lane boundaries.

sol-6.1.text:
Construction is a great example of why driving requires more than following a map. The map might tell you that a lane continues straight, but the cones are telling you that the road has changed. And a person directing traffic may be telling you to do something different from what the traffic light would normally allow.

So you need to bring those signals together. You have to perceive the cones and barriers, understand where the drivable space is, and recognize that a person is directing traffic and interpret their gestures in context. Then you have to plan a safe path while accounting for what the other vehicles and pedestrians might do.

A big part of this is handling uncertainty. If the direction isn’t clear, the vehicle needs to slow down, leave room, and potentially wait. We use these kinds of situations to evaluate the whole system, because recognizing an individual object is only one piece. The real challenge is turning that understanding into appropriate driving behavior.

r001.rationale: The response says cones indicate the road has changed and discusses finding drivable space, but it does not state that cones may require crossing lane boundaries.
